sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Go's `slices` package sorts ordered values with `slices.Sort` and custom values with `slices.SortFunc`. Older APIs in `sort` remain common, including `sort.Ints`, `sort.Strings`, and `sort.Slice`.

A comparator defines the ordering between two values. For `slices.SortFunc`, a negative result means the first value comes before the second, zero means equal in ordering, and positive means after.

For example, sorting people by age and then name compares ages first; only when ages match does it compare names. This produces deterministic output for equal ages.

Most sort helpers rearrange the slice in place. Copy first when callers need the original order, and remember that comparator cost is paid many times.

sections.title: The practical decision: sorting collections in Go
sections.content:
The useful question is not whether sorting collections in Go can be used, but which requirement makes it the clearest and safest fit. That decision includes its cost and its failure boundary.

Stability matters only for elements equal under the active comparison. It is especially useful when applying sorts from secondary key to primary key, or when the original order has business meaning. An unstable sort can be faster or use different resources and is sufficient when equal items are interchangeable.

sections.title: Why the failure happens: sorting collections in Go
sections.content:
Failures around sorting collections in Go usually come from one incorrect assumption about ownership, state, ordering, or lifetime. Finding that assumption is more useful than adding a defensive line at random.

A valid comparison is antisymmetric and transitive in practical terms: if A belongs before B and B before C, A must belong before C. Subtraction-based integer comparators can overflow for extreme values; direct comparisons avoid that problem. Tests should include equal keys and extremes.

sections.title: The important trade-off: sorting collections in Go
sections.content:
sorting collections in Go and writing a sorting algorithm by hand solve related problems, but they expose different guarantees. The best choice follows from the guarantee the program actually needs.

`slices.Sort` is the shortest route for ordered types. `slices.SortFunc` supports structs and alternate orders with compile-time types. `sort.Slice` uses a closure over a slice of any type and remains widely seen. Hand-written sorting adds much more surface for off-by-one and partition errors.
